opus-5.5.text:
I think the data bottleneck is one of the most fundamental questions right now, and it's often misunderstood. Many people treat it as simply "we're running out of internet text," but there are several layers to it.

The first layer is quantity. High-quality natural text produced by humans is finite. Over the past few years, scaling laws worked partly because we kept adding compute and kept finding more tokens to feed the model. If tokens stop growing while compute keeps growing, the efficiency of that recipe drops. So the question becomes: when the supply of fresh, high-quality tokens flattens, how do you keep turning compute into intelligence?

The second layer is quality and distribution. Not all tokens are equal. A large share of web data is repetitive or shallow, and it doesn't teach the model much about reasoning, long-horizon planning, or rigorous thinking. The data that actually drives capability, such as careful derivations, high-quality code, or step-by-step problem solving, is a small fraction. So even before we run out of data in absolute terms, we run out of the most useful kind of data.

The third layer, which I think matters most, is that much of the knowledge we want models to have was never written down. Humans learn by acting, trying things, failing, and getting feedback. The internet captures the results of that process, not the process itself. A model trained only on static text sees answers without the exploration that produced them.

So my view is that the way forward isn't only finding more text. A few directions matter.

One is token efficiency: getting more learning out of each token through better architectures, better optimizers, and better training recipes. If you can make each token worth more, you effectively expand your data.

Another is having models generate their own data, especially through reinforcement learning. When a model attempts a problem, gets a verifiable signal, and learns from that, it's producing new training signal that didn't exist on the internet. This is why reasoning and agentic training have become so important. In a sense, the model shifts from imitating human data to exploring and creating its own experience.

The third is interaction with environments, letting models use tools, write and run code, and operate in real tasks. That's a source of data that can scale with compute rather than with how much humans have written.

So I'd say the data bottleneck is real, but it's also a signal that the paradigm is shifting. The first phase was about compressing the internet. The next phase is about letting models learn from their own experience. Whoever handles that transition well will be in a strong position.

r001.rationale: It says high-quality human text is finite and describes the supply of fresh, high-quality tokens flattening, which conveys an approximately constant supply.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss multimodal data or whether it improves a language model’s intelligence in text.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the data bottleneck is real, but it's often described in a slightly misleading way. People frame it as "we're running out of tokens on the internet," as if the problem were just the raw count. The deeper issue is that the amount of *high-quality, high-information-density* data grows much more slowly than our ability to consume it with compute. Compute has been scaling at a pace that data simply can't match, because data is produced by human civilization at roughly a fixed rate.

So if you look at the scaling laws from a few years ago, the implicit assumption was that data and compute could be scaled together more or less indefinitely. What we've found is that you hit a wall where you can keep adding GPUs, but you're essentially re-reading the same corpus. Doing more epochs helps a little, but with diminishing returns, and eventually the model starts to memorize rather than generalize.

The way I understand it, this pushes the field in two directions at once. One is about efficiency: how much capability can you extract per token? Better architectures, better tokenization, better curriculum, better filtering. Not all tokens are equal, and we've probably been quite wasteful. The second direction is about creating new data, and this is where I think the more interesting shift is happening. Synthetic data, self-play, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards — these are all ways of letting the model generate its own training signal in domains like math and code where correctness can be checked. In those domains, the bottleneck becomes compute again rather than data, which is a much more comfortable place to be.

But I want to be careful here. Synthetic data works well where there's a verifier. For things like world knowledge, taste, judgment, or culture, you can't just generate more of it and check it mechanically. So I'd say the bottleneck isn't uniform. It's being solved quickly in some areas and will remain a genuine constraint in others. And honestly, that asymmetry is going to shape what kinds of capabilities improve fastest over the next few years — models will get much stronger at reasoning and coding before they get proportionally better at things that depend on scarce, un-verifiable human data.

r001.rationale: The response says high-quality, high-information-density data grows much more slowly than compute and that data is produced by civilization at roughly a fixed rate, characterizing its supply as approximately constant.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss multimodal data or whether it improves intelligence in text.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between running out of data and running out of useful information for learning. If you keep increasing model size and compute while training on essentially the same pool of text, eventually the marginal benefit declines. There may still be a lot of text available, but much of it is repetitive or adds very little new information.

So the bottleneck is partly about quantity, but also about quality and the training objective. Can the model learn more from the data it already has? Can we introduce more diverse sources, or create tasks that require more than predicting what someone has already written?

Synthetic data is one possible direction, but generating more tokens doesn’t automatically solve the problem. If a model simply reproduces what it already knows, that can reinforce its limitations. It becomes more interesting when generation is coupled with verification or feedback—for example, attempting a problem and checking whether the solution works. Then you have a mechanism for selecting useful experience.

In that sense, I see the data bottleneck as a question of how we move from consuming a fixed collection of human-produced text toward a process that can continually produce useful learning signals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the data bottleneck has several layers. The most obvious one is that high-quality text on the internet is finite. If we keep increasing model size and compute, we eventually can’t increase the amount of useful training data at the same rate.

But the deeper question is how much a model can learn from the data it already has. Humans can read a textbook and then work through problems, test ideas, and learn from mistakes. Pretraining mostly asks a model to predict the next token. That gives us a very scalable learning signal, but it doesn’t necessarily extract everything that could be learned from the material.

So I wouldn’t frame the problem only as finding more text. We also need better ways to learn: improving data quality, using a better curriculum, and allowing models to interact with environments where they can get feedback.

Synthetic data can help, but generating more text by itself doesn’t guarantee new knowledge. The important question is where the additional learning signal comes from. If a model generates a solution and we can check whether it works—for example, by running a program—then we have a way to improve beyond simply imitating existing text. In that sense, the bottleneck may gradually shift from access to text toward access to reliable feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says high-quality internet text is finite and that useful training data cannot keep growing at the same rate as model size and compute, conveying an effectively capped supply.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss multimodal data or whether it improves a language model’s intelligence in text.
